Topic descriptions under several scores: Levebee mathematics feedback

honets

2026-09-06

The same corpus the sbert package uses in its “Semantic Topics in Levebee AI Mathematics Feedback” vignette, clustered as a hypergraph and described with hg_keywords() under several scores at once. Every number and bar is recomputed at knit time.

The corpus and its embeddings

sbert::feedback_translations holds 8,757 AI-generated feedback messages from the Levebee mathematics application, translated into English. The sbert vignette deduplicates them and works with the first 600 distinct messages, whose all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings ship precomputed with that package. Using the same 600 messages and the same vectors keeps this document offline and directly comparable to the sbert topics.

sample <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "feedback_embeddings.rds",
                              package = "sbert"))
str(sample, max.level = 1)
List of 5
 $ text          : chr [1:600] "Do you know what “one more” means?" "There should be two more in the red than in the blue." "If it’s not a person, what could it be?" "What does “everyone after the first one” mean?" ...
 $ n             : int [1:600] 2 3 2 1 2 1 1 2 1 2 ...
 $ embeddings    : num [1:600, 1:384] -0.0157 0.0108 -0.0847 -0.0509 0.0766 -0.0526 0.036 -0.004 0.0395 0.0728 ...
 $ model_id      : chr "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
 $ model_revision: chr "1110a243fdf4706b3f48f1d95db1a4f5529b4d41"

sample$text is the 600 messages and sample$embeddings their 600 x 384 MiniLM matrix, one row per message in the same order. Both go straight into the constructors; documents are numbered doc_1 to doc_600 on both sides.

Two hypergraphs, one partition

The clustering uses the semantic geometry: each message plus its ten nearest neighbours in embedding space is one hyperedge (construction = "knn"), and hg_cluster() cuts the hypergraph Laplacian’s spectral embedding into six groups, the count the sbert vignette settles on by coherence.

hg_knn <- text_hypergraph(sample$text, construction = "knn", k = 10,
                          embeddings = sample$embeddings)
hg_knn
Text hypergraph: 600 documents (kNN embedding hyperedges: k = 10, cosine)
Hyperedges: 600 (kNN neighborhoods); sizes 11-11, median 11
topics <- hg_cluster(hg_knn, k = 6, seed = 1)
table(topics$cluster)

Cluster 1 Cluster 2 Cluster 3 Cluster 4 Cluster 5 Cluster 6 
       42        42       247       181        47        41

The kNN hypergraph has no words in it, so the description step uses the lexical view of the same 600 messages: the bag-of-words document hypergraph, whose token layer carries the counts, weights and per-document vocabulary that the keyword scores need. Any partition whose names are these documents can be described with it.

hg_bag <- text_hypergraph(sample$text, weight = "tfidf",
                          stop_words = stop_words_en(), min_count = 2L)
hg_bag
Text hypergraph: 600 documents, 186 words (documents as nodes, weight = tfidf)
Hyperedges: 186 (words); sizes 1-173, median 9

Four keyword views of the same six topics

hg_keywords() ranks each cluster’s words under the score named in type; several types at once return one block of rows per score:

  • frequency – what the topic says most (raw counts);
  • ctfidf – what the topic alone says (Grootendorst’s class-based tf-idf, the BERTopic representation);
  • centrality – which words sit at the centre of the topic’s own word hypergraph (words as nodes, the topic’s messages as hyperedges; clique eigenvector centrality);
  • attention – which words the HyperGAT classifier attends to when it learns to predict the topic label from the message: the first attention layer’s node-level weights (the layer that attends over the word embeddings), summed over the topic’s messages.

The first three are cheap and deterministic. The fourth needs : hg_hypergat(what = "attention") trains the network on the cluster labels and returns every message’s per-word attention, which hg_keywords(type = "attention") sums per topic.

views <- hg_keywords(hg_bag, topics, n = 6,
                     type = c("frequency", "ctfidf", "centrality"))
hg_keywords(hg_bag, topics, n = 6, collapse = TRUE,
            type = c("frequency", "ctfidf", "centrality"))

                         seed = 1, what = "attention")

Two facts about this table are worth checking before trusting the column. First, the network was trained to predict the cluster labels, so its attention explains this partition; its agreement with the labels on all 600 messages is the number to look at. Second, attention_2, the second layer’s weights, is uniform within every one-sentence message by construction (all of a document’s words receive the same first-layer output when the document has a single hyperedge), which is why the keyword score uses the first layer. Within a message the first layer does discriminate (“red” gets more than “should” or “two” below), but summed over a topic the score still rises with how often a word occurs, so its rank order is close to frequency’s. The Spearman correlation between the two, over all (topic, word) pairs, is computed here rather than asserted:

fit <- hg_hypergat(sample$text, labels = topics, epochs = 10, seed = 1)
mean(fit$predicted == fit$label)
[1] 0.9583333
subset(attention, node == "doc_2")
     node   word attention attention_2 n_edges
502 doc_2   blue 0.2313071        0.25       1
503 doc_2    red 0.3073240        0.25       1
504 doc_2 should 0.2300997        0.25       1
505 doc_2    two 0.2312691        0.25       1
both <- hg_keywords(hg_bag, topics, n = Inf, scores = attention,
                    type = "frequency")
paired <- merge(subset(both, type == "frequency"),
                subset(both, type == "attention"),
                by = c("cluster", "word"), suffixes = c("_freq", "_att"))
cor(paired$score_freq, paired$score_att, method = "spearman")
[1] 0.9150167

The figure: one panel per topic and score

plot() on the keyword table draws horizontal bars of the score, one row of panels per topic and one column per score type, each panel with its own word axis, fill colour by type. The three lexical scores side by side:

plot(views)

With the attention view added as a fourth column:

four <- hg_keywords(hg_bag, topics, n = 6, scores = attention,
                    type = c("frequency", "ctfidf", "centrality"))
plot(four)

Reading the disagreement

Where the columns agree, the topic owns its vocabulary: read the choose-a-picture panel (“them”, “choose”, “pick”, “select”) across the row. Where they disagree, each score is telling you something different. Frequency promotes words the whole corpus shares (“one”, “you”); c-TF-IDF demotes them and surfaces the topic’s own terms (“middle”, “top”, “gray”); centrality picks the words that co-occur with the most other words inside the topic, which favours the hub of a template (“picture”, “pictures”); attention is whatever the classifier found diagnostic for the topic label, and summed per topic it stays close to frequency (the correlation above), so read it as a frequency count re-weighted by what the classifier used. None is the keyword list. A topic is characterised by the set, and the figure is the compact way to read the set.

These word lists resemble the ones printed in the sbert vignette for the same 600 messages (its topic 1, for instance, is “picture”, “pictures”, “choose”). That is a reading of the two documents side by side, not a computed comparison: sbert’s topic model is not run here, and no agreement statistic between the two partitions is reported.
